title: Launch out into the deep (Luke 5:1–11)
hook: Peter has fished all night for nothing and lets down the nets once more

segments.voice: Yesterday: temptation, three offers in the desert and three answers from scripture. Not by bread alone.

Morning on the lake of Genesareth, the Sea of Galilee. Two boats pulled up on the shore, the fishermen out of them, washing their nets. Simon and his partners have worked from dark to dawn and caught nothing. Not a small catch: nothing. They're tired, and they want to go home. Then a crowd arrives, pressing around a teacher, and the teacher steps into Simon's boat.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `WASHING THE EMPTY NETS.` → `A TEACHER STEPS INTO THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Jesus asks Simon to push out a little from the land, and teaches the crowd from the boat. Then he turns to Simon and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon is the expert here. He knows the lake, and he's just spent the whole night on it. His answer is honest, and a little tired: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." That but is the hinge. Not because I think it'll work. Because you said so. The nets fill so full they start to break. They wave to their partners in the other boat, James and John, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Simon doesn't celebrate. He falls at Jesus's knees: depart from me, for I am a sinful man. The catch has frightened him, not with danger, but with nearness. Jesus answers: fear not, from now on you'll be catching people. They bring the boats to land, leave everything, and follow him. In the Latin Bible the line opens with three short words, duc in altum, and Pope John Paul the Second used them to open the new millennium, calling the whole Church to launch out into the deep. Simon, of course, is the one the Church will call Peter.
screen: `LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP.` · `NOTHING ALL NIGHT. BUT AT THY WORD.` · `NETS BREAKING, BOATS SINKING.` · `DEPART FROM ME. FEAR NOT.` · then, large: `DUC IN ALTUM.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that you've stopped trying at: a conversation that never goes well, a habit you keep failing to start, a hope you put down. Hold it next to Simon's sentence: I've worked all night and caught nothing, but I'll let down the net. If you pray, offer the trying to God.
Draught. An old word for a catch of fish: what filled Simon's nets when he tried once more at Jesus's word.
Your line: but at thy word. Not sure it'll work, and letting down the net anyway. Six days into week five.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass in the Lectionary's year of Luke, and "duc in altum" is a much-quoted motto since John Paul II used it in his 2001 letter for the new millennium.

chat.says: What did Simon do when Jesus told him to fish again after a bad night?
options: He said: we caught nothing, but at your word I'll let down the net.
He refused, since he knew the lake far better, and went home to sleep.
He sent his partners out instead, since he was sure nothing was there.
chat.meaning: Simon, tired and expert, said: at thy word I will let down the net. Not because it would work, but because Jesus said so.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 5:4 and 5:5 given from memory; confirm. The teach screen paraphrases 5:5 as 'we toiled all night' to avoid British spelling in a screen head; confirm acceptable.
'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man' and 'from now on you'll be catching people' (5:8, 5:10) are paraphrased.
The Vulgate of Luke 5:4 reads 'Duc in altum, et laxate retia vestra in capturam'; confirm.
Night fishing as the normal practice on the lake: widely stated; confirm.
John Paul II, Novo Millennio Ineunte (January 6, 2001), opens with and returns to 'Duc in altum'; confirm section numbers.
